newsitem.title: USA: Digital Millicent takes milli-step forward.
newsitem.headline: Digital Millicent takes milli-step forward.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp announced on Monday that its software system for Internet commerce, "Millicent" has entered the pilot stage and said that it expects to start a second pilot for the general public in July.

Millicent is a direct challenge to the Reston, Va.-based CyberCash, Inc and indirectly competes with the smart-card system, Mondex, that is owned by privately held Mastercard International Inc. Millicent promises to allow millions of Internet users to buy and sell information at a fraction of a penny.
"We anticipate that the major audience will be the consumer market," DEC's vice president of business development Jay Zager said in a telephone interview.

In the Millicent environment, consumers will have a broker, probably a bank or on-line service provider, who will issue them scrip for their electronic wallet and a list of content providers, publishers, news services, online games and entertainment, rating services, how-to guides, etc. where they can spend the scrip.
Brokers will make money on the float, Zager said.
DEC said that content providers so far include Reuters America, a unit of Reuters Holdings Plc, InfoSeek Corp Corp and TeleDenmark, the public telephone and telegraph company of Denmark.

A user buys information with each click of the mouse and a running log keeps track of how much scrip users have available in their electronic wallets. To complete the transaction, Millicent software converts what DEC called the universal scrip into an information vendor's own scrip.
The design provides sufficient security without the heavy communications and processor overhead that higher-priced online transactions require, DEC said.
At a penny or less, DEC hopes users will focus on the content of the information rather than the cost.
But Ira Machefsky, an analyst for the Giga group, noted that a number of content providers "do not sell it (information) for pennies....They do it for a pretty penny."

What concerned Machefsky was whether "there is a sufficient and robust business model...On-line publishers have found that people don't want to pay to subscribe, but maybe people are willing to pay as you read...There is a potentially huge demand for this product."
Karen Epper, an analyst with Forrester, said both Millicent and CyberCash had their drawbacks because they are not smart- cards.

"I am supposed to pay my financial institution for cash that I can only use on-line? Why can't I carry my money around and use it both in the virtual and the real world," Epper said. She sees the smart-card, popular in Europe and beginning to grow in North America as "a much better solution for electronic commerce."

"It's a card that has stored value and the value works in both the virtual world and the real world...And when I spend $5 that $5 gets credited to the merchant and debited from my card. There's no middleman and nobody is making money off the float," she said.
